INTRODUCTION

  • The chest contains vital organs.
  • Damage to vital organs threatens life.
  • Most common consequence is hypoxia.
  • Chest injuries result in a significant number of deaths each year.
  • One in every 4 cases of trauma death caused by chest injury.
  • Mechanism of injury :

1) Blunt chest trauma

  • Most common cause of serious chest injuries.
    • Post RTA, falls, direct blows, and crushing injuries.
    • Many injuries are not immediately apparent in physical exam.

2) Penetrating trauma

  • Immediate result can be severe bleeding or impaired breathing.
    • Any chest wound can involve underlying organ injury.
    • No matter how superficial it looks.
    • Injuries to the heart, lungs, and great vessels can quickly lead to shock and cardiac arrest.

3) Iatrogenic

Mechanism of injury : :

Notes

Overview & Mechanisms

The chest houses the organs responsible for ventilation, oxygenation, and circulation. Injury here can trigger a cascade from reversible physiologic derangement to irreversible deterioration and death. Chest injury accounts for roughly 1 in 4 trauma deaths, making it one of the highest-yield systems in trauma assessment.

CategoryKey Features
BluntMost common cause of serious chest injury. Causes: MVCs, falls, direct blows, crush injuries. Internal injuries may be initially occult and declare themselves later.
PenetratingStab or gunshot wounds. Severity depends on weapon/projectile size, force/velocity, distance, trajectory, and number of injuries. May directly injure the heart → shock/arrest. Bleeding and respiratory compromise are usually more immediately apparent, and unstable patients most often require exploration.
IatrogenicE.g. subclavian central-line insertion → injury to the subclavian artery, lung, or diaphragm → massive hemothorax/pneumothorax. Uncommon but preventable.
MECHANISM CONCEPT
High-energy force must pass through the chest-wall barrier (skin → muscle → ribs/sternum) before reaching the lungs, heart, and great vessels. Injury may be direct, compressive, or due to rapid acceleration/deceleration.
★ HIGH-YIELD
Mechanism and speed of injury help predict internal damage — sudden high-speed deceleration produces the greatest shear forces (classic setup for traumatic aortic injury).
Notes

Initial Trauma Assessment

Primary Survey

Follow the ABCDE principles:

Airway + cervical spine protection — assume a c-spine injury until proven otherwise.
Breathing — inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, respiratory rate, SpO₂; give high-flow O₂ when required.
Circulation — assess BP/pulse and hemorrhage; obtain routine bloods + crossmatch, start fluids/blood as indicated. A patient who can answer questions appropriately has, by definition, a patent airway. Examine the chest anteriorly and posteriorly — always inspect the back during the log roll, since important injuries or bleeding can otherwise be missed.
DEFINITION
The primary survey identifies and treats immediately life-threatening problems. Once the patient is stable, move to the secondary survey: a systematic head-to-toe exam plus further investigation.
⚠ DO NOT DELAY
Do not delay transfer to a trauma center, or transfer to the OR, for nonessential imaging. An unstable/hypotensive patient with an immediately treatable cause should go straight to resuscitation and definitive management — not to CT/MRI.
Notes

Penetrating / Impaled Chest Injuries

Any penetrating chest wound may injure the underlying:

Lung / pleura
Heart
Diaphragm
Great vessels
Esophagus
Stomach / liver
⚠ IMPALED OBJECTS
Never remove an impaled object in the ER. It may be tamponading an injured vessel or organ — removal can trigger catastrophic hemorrhage. Stabilize the patient and the object, and remove it under controlled conditions during operative exploration.

If the injury clearly requires exploration, imaging is useful only if it will change immediate management — do not delay necessary surgery to obtain it. Before the OR, alert anesthesia and any specialties that may be needed early: thoracic, cardiac, vascular, GI/general surgery. Cardiac injury may require cardiopulmonary bypass/perfusion support.

  • Signs and symptoms
    • Most common symptoms: pain and difficulty breathing.
    • Signs are obvious injury to the chest wall ( looking at both the front and back of the chest).
    • Note any subcutaneous emphysema, or air present under the skin
  • Assessment

Follow all steps in the assessment of the trauma patient:

  • Primary survey( A. Airway B. Breathing C. Circulation).
    • Resuscitation.
    • Detailed secondary survey (CXR , ABG ,ECG , CT Chest , Aortogram).
Notes

Surgical (Subcutaneous) Emphysema

Subcutaneous / surgical emphysema = air within the subcutaneous tissues, producing swelling with characteristic crepitus. May cause marked swelling of the chest, neck, and face, and if severe can extend to the groin or lower body. It may occur with or without a pneumothorax.

CXR FINDINGS
Air outlines the soft tissues; muscle fibers that are normally poorly visible may become outlined by air.
  • Management
    • Ensure patient has adequate oxygenation and perfusion
    • Provide high-flow oxygen, ventilating when necessary
    • Halt any obvious bleeding
    • Support circulation when needed
    • Rapidly transport patient to definitive care
  • Life threatening chest injury identified in the primary survey:

1) Airway obstruction.

2) Flial chest.

3) Tension pneumothorax.

4) Open pneumothorax.

5) Massive hemothorax.

6) Cardiac tamponade.

  • Stable after an MVA, then mild left chest pain with hyper-resonance → traumatic pneumothorax (not primary — there is trauma; not tension — he is stable). 441
  • Tension pneumothorax causes obstructive shock. 442 434
  • The sign that best separates tension pneumothorax from cardiac tamponade → breath sounds (absent in tension; both have hypotension and raised JVP). 438 ×3
  • Potentially lethal chest injury:

1) Traumatic aortic rupture.

2) Myocardial contusion.

3) Tracheal bronchial injury.

4) Rupture diaphragm.

5) Esophageal trauma.

6) Pulmonary contusion.

  • Trauma patient whose NG tube and stomach bubble are seen in the left chest → diaphragmatic rupture. 439
Notes

Causes

SourceMechanism
Respiratory (≈85%)Rib fracture → lung/visceral pleural injury → air escapes. Air collects in the pleural cavity (pneumothorax) or dissects through the chest wall (subcutaneous emphysema). Also: postoperative air leak (especially a blocked/kinked/compressed chest tube), barotrauma from positive-pressure ventilation/high PEEP, and severe ventilated asthma. Exclude major tracheobronchial injury if emphysema is massive or rapidly developing.
Upper GI / esophagealIatrogenic esophageal perforation after endoscopy/dilatation (especially a diseased esophagus, e.g. achalasia or esophageal cancer); duodenal perforation during ERCP/sphincterotomy (duodenum is vulnerable due to its thin wall); Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophageal rupture).
Notes

Esophageal Rupture / Boerhaave Syndrome

Escaped air/fluid may enter the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum), the pleural cavities (pneumothorax/pleural fluid, often left- sided), or the subcutaneous tissues (surgical emphysema).

⚠ RAPID DETERIORATION TIMELINE
~4–6 h: mediastinitis may develop • ~8 h: severe mediastinitis • later: severe sepsis and hemodynamic instability with very high mortality.
Early esophageal rupture is a surgical emergency — operative management is emphasized, particularly within the first ~12 hours.
Notes

Management of Subcutaneous Emphysema

There is no single treatment — manage ABC + the underlying cause. Observe if the patient is stable and the emphysema is nonprogressive.

URGENT INTERVENTION IF
Vital signs deteriorate / hemodynamic instability develops, or the emphysema is rapidly expanding (tracking around the whole body, up to the neck).
Respiratory source (most common, ~85%) / pneumothorax → insert a chest tube and apply suction as appropriate; confirm any existing drain is patent.
Large ongoing air leak may need an additional chest tube; severe bilateral disease may need bilateral drainage.
Massive unexplained emphysema after intubation/ventilation → exclude major airway injury, including with bronchoscopy.
Persistent major lung/airway injury that keeps expanding despite two chest tubes and cannot be controlled → proceed to operative exploration (thoracotomy).
Notes

Life-Threatening vs. Potentially Lethal Injuries

CategoryExamples
Immediately life-threatening found on primary surveyTreated immediately — e.g. airway obstruction, which can rapidly kill the patient.
Potentially lethal may emerge on secondary surveyTraumatic aortic injury/rupture · myocardial contusion · tracheobronchial injury · diaphragmatic rupture · esophageal injury (isolated traumatic esophageal injury is very rare). Associated spinal/vertebral or vascular injuries may coexist.
  • Rule out on the primary survey → open pneumothorax (not lung contusion, aortic disruption or diaphragm rupture — those are secondary-survey injuries). 431 ×3
  • Should be dealt with in the primary survey → massive haemothorax (aortic and oesophageal injuries are secondary-survey). 437
Notes

Rib Fractures

The most common chest injury.

★ MCQ — AGE PATTERN
More common in adults than children: children's ribs are more cartilaginous/compliant, so they fracture less easily. The elderly are at increased risk from osteoporosis. Young patients usually need substantial trauma to fracture a rib — but because their compliant chest wall transmits force efficiently to the lung, children can sustain more pulmonary contusion despite fewer fractures.

Commonly involved ribs: approximately the 5th–9th, reflecting relatively poor bony protection in this zone.

The doctor (and every past key) uses the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line. The current ATLS (10th ed.) prefers the 4th–5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line in adults (thinner chest wall, fewer failures); the 2nd ICS MCL remains for children. For this exam, answer 2nd ICS MCL.
Notes

Location & Associated Injuries

Rib LevelSignificance
Lower ribs (8–12)Suspect associated abdominal/retroperitoneal solid-organ injury — liver, spleen, kidney — despite the diaphragm's protective position.
1st–2nd ribsFracture = marker of high-energy trauma, since these ribs are short, thick, and protected by the clavicle/shoulder girdle/muscles. Actively search for associated aortic, bronchial, and mediastinal/great- vessel injuries.
Notes

Clinical Features

Pain
Chest-wall tenderness / instability
Deformity
Discoloration / bruising
May coexist with pneumothorax or hemothorax
  • Not an indication for a chest tube → pneumoperitoneum (chylothorax, pneumothorax and haemothorax are). 437
Notes

Management

ABC + oxygenation/resuscitation as required. ~95% are treated conservatively.

★ MCQ — ANALGESIA IS CENTRAL TO TREATMENT
Inadequate pain control → poor inspiration/cough → retained secretions → atelectasis/consolidation/pneumonia. This risk is greatest in elderly patients, smokers, and those with COPD/asthma/underlying lung disease.
Best analgesia: thoracic epidural — long-acting local anesthetic (e.g. bupivacaine) ± fentanyl for synergistic analgesia. Monitor patients on epidural therapy, and avoid an excessively high block, since respiratory function (diaphragm) depends on the phrenic roots C3–C5 (mainly C4).
Alternatives: patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) if epidural is unavailable; IV morphine/opioid analgesia; local anesthetic infiltration (e.g. lidocaine).

Once pain is controlled, encourage:

Deep breathing
Coughing
Incentive spirometry
Chest physiotherapy
Mobilization / walking

Treat any associated pneumothorax or hemothorax separately.

1 Rib fractures are the most common chest injury; think liver/spleen/kidney with lower rib fractures and great-vessel/bronchial
injury with 1st–2nd rib fractures.
2 Thoracic epidural is the best-evidence analgesia — poor analgesia is the pathway to pneumonia.
3 Watch the block height: phrenic roots are C3–C5 (mainly C4).
Notes

Tracheal or Major Bronchial Rupture

Very rarely iatrogenic — mostly due to blunt injury.

SYMPTOMS / SIGNS
Dyspnea · cyanosis · hemoptysis · crepitus · surgical emphysema · hemodynamic instability.

X-ray: massive pneumothorax with a large volume of air.

A chest tube is inserted, but the patient does not improve and the lung fails to re-expand → take the patient to the OR and open the chest (thoracotomy).

Rib Fracture

  • Most common chest injury.
  • More common in adults than children.
  • Especially common in elderly.
  • Ribs form rings, Consider possibility of break in two places.
  • 80-year-old with 2 rib fractures after an MVA → admit and start pain control (elderly = high risk of pneumonia). 439
  • Most commonly 5th to 9th ribs.
  • Poor protection.
  • Fractures of 8th to 12th ribs can damage underlying abdominal solid organs:
    • Liver.
    • Spleen.
    • Kidneys.
  • Fractures of 1st, 2nd ribs require high force.
  • Frequently have injury to aorta or bronchi.
  • 30% will die.
Notes

Traumatic Aortic Injury

Classic mechanism: rapid deceleration — e.g. a high-speed collision that suddenly reduces velocity to zero. Shear forces act where a relatively mobile aortic segment meets a fixed one, classically near the aortic isthmus, just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery / at the ligamentum arteriosum.

An initial intimal tear allows blood to dissect between the vessel wall layers, forming a false lumen/hematoma that may progress to complete rupture. The injury may be immediately catastrophic, or initially small and present later.

CXR CLUES
Widened mediastinum
Apical cap / pleural apical hematoma
1st / 2nd rib fracture
Displaced mediastinal structures (NG tube/esophagus or left main bronchus)

Definitive evaluation: CT with IV contrast / CT angiography (conventional aortography was used historically). Historical treatment was open surgical replacement/prosthesis; modern management increasingly uses endovascular stent-grafting where appropriate.

  • Local swelling and tenderness may be the only sign of a broken rib.
    • Can be very painful.
    • Patients often presents with guarding and shallow breathing.
    • Management
    • Move the patient carefully to prevent the bone ends from puncturing the lung.
    • Administer O2.
    • Allow patient to self-splint by assuming the most comfortable position possible.
    • Encourage patient to limit movement.
    • Analgesia like Morphine, PCA, Epidural.

Flial Chest

  • Flail segment
    • When three or more ribs are broken in two or more places, a rib-cage segment may detach from the rest.
    • Flail segment is free floating.
    • Paradoxical movement: movement of flail segment in opposite direction of the rest of the chest wall .
    • Paradoxical movement can significantly impair breathing and cause injury to the underlying lung.
  • Paradoxical chest-wall segment after a car accident → initial management: pain control and oxygen (not a chest tube, thoracotomy or fixation first). 442
  • True about flail chest → paradoxical breathing movement (it needs ≥ 3 ribs in ≥ 2 places, not 5; patients are symptomatic; thoracotomy is rarely needed). 438
Notes

Flail Chest

Flail chest = ≥3 adjacent ribs fractured in ≥2 places, creating a free flail segment. Fractures may involve the anterior, lateral, or posterior portion of the same ribs.

CHARACTERISTIC FINDING
Paradoxical chest-wall movement in a spontaneously breathing patient: on inspiration the normal chest expands outward while the flail segment moves inward; on expiration the normal chest recoils inward while the flail segment moves outward. Positive-pressure ventilation ± muscle relaxation can abolish or mask this paradoxical movement.

May coexist with pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary contusion.

Notes

Management

Many cases are managed conservatively: excellent analgesia, respiratory physiotherapy, treatment of associated injuries, and ventilatory support if required. Rib healing generally takes about 4–6 weeks. Short-term ventilation may be used in severe cases to overcome pain/paradoxical motion while complications are treated.

★ MCQ — INDICATIONS FOR SURGICAL RIB FIXATION
Severely displaced fractures
Severe/florid flail segment or paradoxical movement
Bilateral flail chest
Elderly patient / severe injury
Significant underlying lung disease (e.g. COPD)
Failure to wean/extubate, or repeated extubation failure/desaturation
Already undergoing thoracotomy for another major chest injury (fixation done at the same operation)
Modern practice increasingly favors early fixation in selected patients to speed recovery and reduce prolonged ventilation. Fixation uses plates (including titanium systems); Kirschner-wire/skeletal-traction techniques are obsolete. Presentation delayed by months, after the fracture has solidly united, is difficult to correct.
  • Management
    • Quickly stabilize flail segment by placing gloved hand over injured area.
    • After manual stabilization, place folded universal dressing over segment and tape securely.
    • Fixation ( External, Internal).
  • Post Traumatic Pneumothorax

Types:

1) Opened pneumothorax.

2) Close pneumothorax.

Notes

Pneumothorax

Traumatic pneumothorax may be closed or open.

CXR FINDINGS
Absent peripheral lung markings; a visible pleural/lung edge representing the collapsed lung; increased radiolucency. Degree of collapse may be obvious — CT is not routinely required just to diagnose an obvious pneumothorax.
  • Open pneumothorax
    • A sharp object penetrates the skin on the chest wall.
    • If penetrating object has pierced pleura, outside air can enter the thoracic cavity.
    • As the volume of air in the thoracic cavity expands, the lung starts to collapse .
    • Air within the pleural space is called a pneumothorax
    • As air passes in and out of an open wound, it can create a sucking-type sound.
    • Sucking chest wound means possibility of pneumothorax.
    • Signs of pneumothorax: difficulty breathing, cyanosis, diminished breath sounds on the affected side.
  • Open penetrating left chest wound, laboured breathing, BP 100/70 → chest tube thoracostomy. 430

Open pneumothorax

  • Management
    • Cover open chest wounds with occlusive dressing
    • Gloved hand is an effective temporary occlusive dressing
    • Secure dressing on three sides
    • High-flow oxygen
    • Transport with unaffected side slightly elevated
  • Open chest wound → 3-sided dressing. 431
  • Gunshot with a sucking chest wound, BP 70/30 → keyed initial step three-sided dressing. 434 ×2
  • Tension pneumothorax
    • Build up of pressure in pleural space resulting in decrease in blood pressure.
    • Potentially life-threatening condition that must be treated immediately.
    • Can occur in blunt or penetrating chest trauma.
  • Signs
    • Include all those of a pneumothorax.
    • Jugular venous distension (JVD).
    • If ventilating becomes more difficult, significant lung compression is indicated.

Tension Pneumothorax

  • One-way valve forms in lung or chest wall
  • Air enters pleural space; cannot leave
  • Air is trapped in pleural space
  • Pressure rises
  • Pressure collapses lung
Notes

Open / Sucking Pneumothorax

Open pneumothorax = a communication between the pleural cavity and atmosphere (stab, gunshot, or surgical/chest-wall wound). Pleural pressure is normally negative (roughly −6 to −12 mmHg, more negative with forceful inspiration/cough), so atmospheric air is drawn into the pleural space through the open wound. Air can enter from two sources at once: the external chest-wall opening and an injured/lacerated lung.

⚠ VALVE EFFECT
A valve-like wound may let air in but prevent its escape, rapidly producing a tension pneumothorax — potentially within minutes.
★ EXAM — 3-SIDED OCCLUSIVE DRESSING
Temporizing measure when definitive chest drainage is not immediately available: place an occlusive dressing over the wound and tape 3 sides, leaving 1 side open. On inspiration the dressing is sucked against the wound, limiting air entry; on expiration the free edge lifts, letting trapped air escape. As soon as chest-tube capability exists, insert a chest tube promptly, cover the wound, and arrange definitive surgical treatment as required.
  • Stab wound to the right chest, BP 80/40, GCS 15 → chest tube insertion first (haemothorax — drain and measure). 438 ×5
Notes

Tension Pneumothorax

A one-way valve mechanism causes progressively trapped pleural air, rising intrathoracic pressure, and lung collapse. The increasing pressure compresses the vena cavae → reduced venous return → ↓ cardiac output → shock/cardiovascular collapse. This can develop especially rapidly during positive-pressure ventilation.

★ VERY IMPORTANT — DIAGNOSIS (CLASSIC OSCE QUESTION)
Tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis. Do not wait for a chest X-ray in a clinically unstable patient — the delay can be fatal. It produces both respiratory compromise and cardiovascular/hemodynamic compromise.
  • MVA, hypotensive, reduced air entry on the right, ABG with hypoxia and respiratory acidosis → needle decompression (don't wait for an X-ray, don't intubate first). 434 ×2 431
Notes

Immediate Management — Needle Decompression

A temporizing emergency measure before definitive tube thoracostomy.

ParameterDetail
Site2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line
TechniqueInsert the needle above the rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle running below it. Landmark via the Angle of Louis → 2nd costal cartilage.
Needle gaugeLarge-bore, approximately 12–14G (14–16G also discussed) — MCQ/OSCE
Needle lengthApproximately 5–7.5 cm; a longer catheter may be required depending on chest-wall thickness — MCQ/OSCE
ConfirmationAudible/obvious gush of air on entering the pleural cavity. Remove the metal needle, leaving the plastic catheter in place temporarily.
Purpose = buy time while preparing definitive chest tube. Definitive treatment is tube thoracostomy / chest tube.
  • First-line treatment → needle decompression, 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, then a chest tube. 432 ×3 436 429 428 442
  • Ideal chest-tube site → 5th intercostal space (4th space above the 5th rib), mid-axillary line. 437 ×2 427
  • Landmark that finds the site quickly → level of the nipple (≈ 4th–5th ICS). 435
  • When inserting a chest tube → full aseptic technique. 436
  • Trapped air pushes heart, lungs away from injured side
  • Both Vena cavae become kinked
  • Blood cannot return to heart
  • Cardiac output falls
  • Sepsis patient 2 hours after a subclavian central line: tachycardia, falling BP and SpO₂ → tension pneumothorax (iatrogenic). 438 ×3
  • Typical tension picture (unstable, resonant, absent breath sounds, trachea shifted away) → tension pneumothorax 437; after an MVA with rib fracture, tracheal deviation and ↓ breath sounds → tension pneumothorax 439; motorbike crash, SpO₂ 85%, hypertympanic left chest, BP 80/40 → tension pneumothorax. 437
  • Side matters: trachea deviated to the LEFT + absent breath sounds/hyper-resonance on the RIGHT → needle decompression on the RIGHT 2nd ICS MCL. 442 439
  • Transfusion of 2 L through a central line — the complication keyed → tension pneumothorax (from line insertion). 437
  • During management of tension pneumothorax, the irrelevant step → confirming the chest tube with CT. 438
  • Tension Pneumothorax

Haemothorax

  • Blood in pleura space
  • Most common result of major chest wall trauma
  • Present in 70 to 80% of penetrating, major non-penetrating chest trauma
Notes

Other Emergency Needle Procedures

Pericardiocentesis for Acute Tamponade

Acute tamponade can occur with only ~100–200 mL of rapidly accumulated blood/fluid, whereas a slowly developing chronic effusion may be tolerated at much larger volumes.

EMERGENCY SUBXIPHOID APPROACH
Entry approximately 1 cm below the xiphoid, 1 cm to the left; needle angled at about 45°, aimed toward the left shoulder tip; advance slowly with monitoring while aspirating. Used as an emergency temporizing maneuver in acute tamponade/trauma.
  • Intubated RTA patient, hard to bag, reduced air entry on the LEFT, trachea to the RIGHT → needle decompression on the LEFT 2nd ICS. 430
  • E-FAST cannot see retroperitoneal haemorrhage (it sees pericardial fluid, intraperitoneal blood and pneumothorax). 431
Notes

Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage (DPL)

Historically performed with a long needle/catheter (lecture cited approximately 18G). Now used far less because of FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma). Before DPL, decompress/empty the bladder and stomach, and direct the catheter toward the pelvis.

  • Stab wound with a picture of tension → needle chest decompression first. 433
  • Blunt chest injury with hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) → pericardiocentesis. 442 ×2
  • Source of bleeding
  • Intercostal vessels
  • Internal mammary vessels
  • Lung parenchyma
  • Broncheal arteries
  • Major pulmonary vessels
  • Heart and great vessels
Notes

Hemothorax

Hemothorax = collection of blood in the pleural cavity. May produce hemorrhagic shock: hypotension, tachycardia, distress/anxiety, and other signs of blood loss.

Sources: intercostal vessels · internal mammary arteries (LIMA/RIMA) · lung parenchyma · major pulmonary vessels · heart/great vessels.

IMAGING
CXR: pleural blood produces radiopacity (not hyperlucency, unlike pneumothorax). CT may further demonstrate hemothorax and lung collapse — assess the mediastinal/soft-tissue window in addition to the lung window.

Hemothorax

  • Management
    • Secure airway
    • Assist breathing with high concentration O2
    • Rapid transport

Indications for Thoracotomy:

  • Initial output is > 1250 ml
  • Initial output is > 1000 ml with hypotension
  • Output > 250 ml/h for 3 hours
Thoracotomy threshold: the slide gives > 1250 mL initial (or > 1000 mL with hypotension) or > 250 mL/h × 3 h; the notes say ≈ 1.5 L or > 200–250 mL/h × 3 h; ATLS uses 1500 mL immediately or 200 mL/h for 2–4 h. All past keys (1600 mL, 1800 mL) are above every threshold.
  • MVA haemothorax, 1800 mL immediately → urgent thoracotomy in the OR (an ED thoracotomy is for the arrested patient). 442
Notes

Management & Operative Thresholds

Resuscitate and insert a chest tube.

FindingAction
Massive initial drainage (~1.5 L)Indicates surgical bleeding → urgent surgical thoracotomy / operative exploration.
Lower initial output (e.g. 500–600 mL), patient stableContinue resuscitation and monitor tube output very closely.
Ongoing bleeding >200–250 mL/hour for 3 consecutive hours= surgical bleed → OR / thoracotomy — ★ high-yield MCQ
GOAL
Intervene before compensated hemorrhage progresses to irreversible hemorrhagic shock.
  • Stab wound on the right side of the chest → initial step insert a chest tube. 434

Chest tube

  • Gunshot haemothorax, chest tube drains 1600 mL → emergent thoracotomy. 439 442
  • Pulmonary contusion
    • Bleeding into the lung itself is a pulmonary contusion
    • Bleeding and edema can impair gas exchange, causing hypoxia and respiratory faliure.
    • Soft crackles may be heard over injury site
    • Chest pain, point tenderness, and localized swelling over area of impact
    • Management
    • Support ventilation as needed
    • Supply high-flow supplemental oxygen
    • Transport to hospital--- ventilation
  • Minor fall, stable, mild SOB, mild pneumothorax → observation with supplemental oxygen. 442
Notes

Pulmonary Contusion

Pulmonary contusion = traumatic bruising/internal hemorrhage of the lung parenchyma. Often associated with rib fractures, flail chest, hemothorax/pneumothorax, and major blunt/penetrating thoracic trauma.

CLINICAL FEATURES
Dyspnea · cyanosis · ↓ SpO₂ · hypoxemia on ABG. Severe disease may impair ventilation and raise CO₂.
⚠ DELAYED PRESENTATION
Does not necessarily appear immediately — radiographic/clinical changes may develop or worsen over several hours, including around 6–12 h after injury.

Usually treated conservatively/supportively. Thoracotomy may still be required for an associated injury — e.g. massive hemothorax or lung laceration from a displaced rib.

  • Flail chest — the false statement: "management is usually by thoracotomy". 427
Notes

Fluid Management

Avoid excessive crystalloid: fluid extravasation into injured lung parenchyma can worsen pulmonary edema and oxygenation. Restrictive fluid replacement is emphasized — give only what is necessary to maintain adequate intravascular volume.

WHY RESTRICTIVE FLUIDS
After several hours, much of an administered crystalloid load leaves the intravascular compartment, whereas colloid/blood products/plasma remain intravascular more effectively. Example: in an ~80 kg patient, use limited maintenance replacement rather than large-volume crystalloid loading — total crystalloid kept around ≤1.5 L in this context. Excess fluid → increasing lung extravasation → worsening contusion and desaturation.
  • Diaphragmatic injury
  • Types

1) Acute blunt injury

2) Acute penetrating injury

3) Chronic diaphragmatic hernia

  • Cardiac contusion
    • Can impair heart’s ability to pump
    • Bleeding into heart tissue can cause heart to beat irregularly
    • Irregular pulse should alert to possibility of a cardiac contusion
    • Diagnosis
    • Fracture sternum
    • ECG----- ST& T abnormality + Dysrhythmias
    • CPK-MB
  • Management
    • High-flow oxygen
    • Ventilation support as needed
    • Support of circulation if appropriate
    • Prompt transport
    • Request ALS backup

Cardiac contusion

  • Pericardial tamponade
    • Bleeding around heart and into pericardial sac that encloses the heart can cause pericardial tamponade
    • Usually results from a penetrating chest trauma with laceration to the heart itself
    • Blood filling the pericardial sac compresses heart, causing blood to back up
    • JVD is a telltale sign of pericardial tamponade
    • Narrowed pulse pressures
  • Pulseless on arrival after a penetrating (stab) wound of the anterior chest, lost the pulse in the ER / pulse 5 minutes ago → emergency (resuscitative) thoracotomy. 441 442
  • Penetrating chest wound with tamponade on eFAST → keyed emergency thoracotomy (surgical repair; pericardiocentesis only temporizes). 442

Pericardial tamponade

  • Management
    • High-flow oxygen
    • Treat patient for shock
    • Transport rapidly to ER
    • Request ALS intercept
    • Notify hospital so staff can properly prepare
  • Aortic injury
    • In sudden decelerations such as high-speed head-on MVCs, body organs are thrown forcefully against the front of the body
    • Most significant tear: aorta
    • If tear is complete, patient will die in minute
  • Management
    • High-flow oxygen
    • Treat patient for shock
    • Transport rapidly to ED
    • Notify hospital so staff can properly prepare
  • Stable stab wound to the right chest, CXR: small pneumothorax + moderate effusion → chest tube. 439

Conclusion

Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 Chest trauma causes ~1 in 4 trauma deaths — three categories: blunt (most common), penetrating, and iatrogenic.
2 Never remove an impaled object in the ER — it may be tamponading a bleed; remove only under controlled operative
conditions.
3 Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis — treat with immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS, midclavicular line,
above the rib), do not wait for imaging.
4 3-sided occlusive dressing for open/sucking pneumothorax — converts a sucking wound into a one-way flutter valve until a
chest tube can be placed.
5 Hemothorax operative thresholds: ~1.5 L initial drainage, or >200–250 mL/hour for 3 consecutive hours → OR/thoracotomy.
6 1st/2nd rib fractures signal high-energy trauma — screen for aortic, bronchial, and great-vessel injury. Lower rib (8–12)
fractures signal possible liver/spleen/kidney injury.
7 Best analgesia for rib fractures/flail chest is a thoracic epidural — poor pain control drives atelectasis and pneumonia.
8 Traumatic aortic injury: rapid deceleration → shear at the aortic isthmus; widened mediastinum on CXR; CT angiography is
definitive; endovascular stent-grafting is now favored.
Flail chest = ≥3 adjacent ribs fractured in ≥2 places, with paradoxical chest-wall movement; most managed conservatively, but know the surgical fixation indications.
Pulmonary contusion: keep fluids restrictive (crystalloid worsens lung edema); changes may not appear for 6–12 hours.
dug:
• Timely imaging (CTA, MRI) to detect vascular & spinal injuries.
  • Surgical repair of vascular, esophageal, & airway injuries.
  • High suspicion for BCVI in blunt trauma cases.
Thoracic Injuries:

Thoracic trauma contributes to 50% of trauma-related deaths due to its impact on airway, circulation, and respiratory function. Rapid identification and management of life-threatening conditions are crucial.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure and assess for tracheal injury, obstruction, or tension pneumothorax.
  • Breathing: Look for flail chest, pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary contusion.
  • Circulation: Identify cardiac tamponade, aortic injury, or massive hemorrhage.
  • Disability (Neurologic): Monitor for spinal cord injury or hypoxia-induced brain dysfunction.
  • Exposure: Examine for penetrating wounds, bruising, subcutaneous emphysema.
Life-Threatening Thoracic Injuries (The “Deadly Six”):

1. Airway obstruction 2. Tension pneumothorax 3. Massive hemothorax 4. Flail chest 5. Open pneumothorax 6. Cardiac tamponade

Abdominal Trauma:

Abdominal trauma is categorized into penetrating and blunt injuries. Early identification and appropriate intervention are key to preventing shock, sepsis, and multiorgan failure.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure airway in unstable patients.
  • Breathing: Monitor for associated thoracic injuries.
